Christopher Columbus was a Genoese navigator who sailed under the Spanish flag and fundamentally altered human history, though not in the way he intended. In 1492, he commanded three ships—the Niña, Pinta, and Santa Maria—on a transatlantic voyage that took seventy days and reached the Caribbean. He believed he could reach Asia by sailing west across the Atlantic, but he drastically underestimated the Earth's circumference and had no idea that the Americas existed.

He landed in the Bahamas in October 1492, convinced he had reached the outer islands of Asia. He never grasped the magnitude of his discovery. He made four Atlantic voyages between 1492 and 1502, and always insisted that he had reached the Asian coast, despite overwhelming geographical evidence to the contrary. Columbus established the colony of La Isabela on Hispaniola in 1494, the first permanent European settlement in the Caribbean. But his tenure as governor was marked by extraordinary brutality. He demanded tribute in gold from indigenous peoples, imposed cruel punishments on colonists, and oversaw the enslavement of thousands of natives. He enslaved indigenous people and sent them back to Spain as human cargo, and when uprisings threatened Spanish control, he responded with military force and systematic violence.

In 1500, after reports of his violent governance reached the Spanish Crown, he was arrested and returned to Spain in chains. He spent his final years petitioning for recognition and payment, dying in relative obscurity. Yet his voyages triggered the Age of Exploration and opened the door to European colonial expansion and conquest. His journey initiated the first sustained contact between Eurasia and the Americas, leading to the Columbian Exchange—the biological, cultural, and epidemiological transformation of both hemispheres. For indigenous peoples of the Caribbean and Americas, his voyage resulted in catastrophe. Diseases, warfare, and enslavement killed an estimated ninety percent of native populations within a century.
